# Comparable

Ordering: which of two values of one type comes first.

```rux
pub interface Comparable {
    func Compare(other: &Self) -> Ordering;
}
```

The bound a generic writes when it needs to sort, search a sorted sequence, or find an extreme. `Self` in the
signature is the implementing type, so a value is only ever ordered against another of its own type.
An implementation must be a total order: exactly one of less, equal or greater holds for any pair; reversing the
operands reverses the answer; and the relation is transitive, for the ordering and for the equality it reports.
A type with a value that compares unordered against everything, the way a floating-point NaN does, cannot promise
this and should not implement it. Algorithms that sort or search assume all three and may otherwise loop, drop
elements, or read past their bounds.
A type implementing both this and [`Equatable`](/docs/api/core/equatable) must keep them agreeable: [`Compare`](/docs/api/core/comparable#compare) reports `Equal` exactly when
[`Equals`](/docs/api/core/equatable#equals) reports true.

## Requirements

<h3 id="compare"><code>Compare</code></h3>

```rux
func Compare(other: &Self) -> Ordering
```

Compares this value against `other`.
Borrows both operands and takes ownership of neither. The reference guarantees that `other` is present.
Returns `Less` when this value comes first, `Greater` when `other` does, and `Equal` when neither does. Cannot
fail: a total order places every pair.

| Name    | Type    | Description                  |
| ------- | ------- | ---------------------------- |
| `other` | `&Self` | the value to compare against |

**Returns**: how this value orders against `other`
